title: ÆTHER: Kolusu (South Indian horror theme)
story: Midnight in an old ancestral house in a village. A swing creaks on its own, anklet bells walk across the empty hall, a woman hums a lullaby nobody should know. The lamp goes out. She is right behind you.

brief.notes: Jithesh 29 Oct: 'i need a horror track, it should kill the person and burn the ass', i.e. the scariest possible horror BGM. Horror the South Indian film way (style, rule 15): a ghost's lullaby melody in a dark raga (Subhapantuvarali-like: minor second, raised fourth, minor sixth, raised seventh) hummed by one female voice with slow gamakam bends; anklet bells (kolusu) as the ghost's footsteps = our own sound palette (rule 9); the udukkai hourglass drum of village possession rituals; the possession frenzy switching into a tisram triplet gallop with tight full-band unison stabs; stop-and-slam jump scares; a korvai ending played three times. Broken Heritage: reversed veena = the creeping riser (once), pitched-down mridangam = the sub thumps, glitch-chopped veena stutters like a flickering lamp. Motif: the lullaby begins with the rising 3-note call (root, minor third, fifth, bent up) and the track ends on it. Rules 9.11-9.13: one-two sounds open with an instant attention grab, layer by layer, a new event every 8-12 s, two composed jump scares (full silence then a slam) plus a key lift. Horror needs real dynamic range, so mastering keeps the silences (no heavy squash).

prompt: Terrifying South Indian horror film background score, instrumental, 75 seconds, the scariest possible: a vengeful ghost in an old village house at midnight. Written exactly the way Tamil and Telugu horror film composers write it, not a Western horror cue. Second zero: a sudden sharp anklet-bell jingle right next to the ear and a deep, wet low boom, then silence except a slow creaking wooden swing and a far heartbeat. A lone, close female voice hums a slow, eerie lullaby, wordless, in a dark raga (minor second, raised fourth, minor sixth, raised seventh) with long sliding bends and trembling grace notes; the lullaby starts with a rising three-note call (root, minor third, fifth, last note bent up). Anklet bells walk slowly from left to right like footsteps in an empty hall. From about 8 seconds one layer at a time: an out-of-tune detuned veena plucked and glitch-stuttered like a flickering oil lamp, a low pitched-down mridangam thump like something heavy behind a door, bowed metal and scraping cello clusters, a slow hourglass ritual drum. At 18 seconds a dead stop, one full second of total silence, then a massive jump-scare stinger: a screaming high string cluster, a huge distorted low hit and a sharp female shriek-like high note. Then the possession ritual: the ritual drum and thavil burst into a fast frantic triplet gallop, tight full-band unison stabs with deep brass and distorted strings, a wordless male chant growling in rhythm, the lullaby melody now played huge and wrong on the low brass, a new terrifying idea every 8 to 10 seconds. At about 45 seconds everything drops to only the lullaby humming, close and slow, a whole step higher, getting closer, breathing, a long reversed veena swell slowly creeping up. Total silence for one beat. Then the biggest jump scare: a giant slam with every instrument, a shrieking choir cluster and pounding drums in triplets, a rhythmic phrase played three times and landing hard. Ending: one anklet-bell jingle, the three-note lullaby call hummed once, right at the ear, then a sudden cut to silence. Real acoustic instruments carry half the sound, dark processed electronics the other half. Huge dynamic range, deep sub bass, wide, cinematic, clean high-end mix. No lyrics, no spoken words, no EDM, no generic Hollywood trailer braams, no white-noise risers, not ambient drone only.
